verses.note: ‘My people’ is covenant language: God claims Israel as his own before the exodus, the law, or the land. The New Testament uses the same language of the church, a people belonging to God (1 Peter 2:9-10).

Paul quotes the formula in its Leviticus form for the church, the temple of the living God (2 Corinthians 6:16). The people God forms by redemption are defined by belonging to him, not by ethnicity or achievement.
On the usual reading, love for God overflows into delight in God's people. The faithful community is the first sphere where devotion to God shows itself.
Rescue leads to the assembly. The sufferer's private deliverance becomes public praise that builds up God's people.

The New Testament takes up the image of a bride prepared and presented to her husband for the church: Paul speaks of Christ presenting the church to himself in splendor (Ephesians 5:27), and Revelation of the bride clothed in fine linen for the marriage of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7-8). The psalm supplies the picture; the application to the church is the New Testament's.

On the Masoretic reading, the king's people come as freewill offerings, volunteers rather than conscripts. Paul's call to present your bodies as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1) describes the same willing self-offering of a people to their king.

The healing of a centuries-old division between brothers is part of the messianic hope. Ezekiel 37:15-22 pictures the two sticks of Judah and Joseph joined into one in God's hand, and Paul describes Christ breaking down the dividing wall of hostility to make one new people (Ephesians 2:14-16).

The phrase ‘they will all know Me’ is central to a long Christian disagreement. Baptist interpreters, for example Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum in Kingdom through Covenant (2012), argue that the new covenant community consists only of those who know the Lord, which supports baptizing believers only. Paedobaptist interpreters (Presbyterian, Reformed, Anglican, Lutheran, and others) argue that the promise is fulfilled in stages, already and not yet, that Hebrews itself warns members of the covenant community against falling away, and that children of believers belong to the covenant as in Israel. Both sides read the same verse with care.

The unity promised is God's work, done in his hand, not a negotiated merger. The New Testament speaks the same way of the church: Christ has made Jew and Gentile one new people, breaking down the dividing wall (Ephesians 2:14-16), and Jesus prays that his people may be one (John 17:21).

The New Testament applies the saints' reign to the church: believers will reign with Christ (2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 20:4) and will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2). Christians differ on how much of this is present and how much awaits Christ's return.

Christians have applied this command differently. The Anabaptist Schleitheim Confession (1527, article 7) and later the Quakers refused all oaths. Augustine, the Reformers, and most churches (Thirty-Nine Articles, article 39; Westminster Confession 22) permit solemn oaths before a magistrate, noting that God swears (Hebrews 6:13-17) and Paul calls God as witness (Romans 1:9; Galatians 1:20), and read Jesus as forbidding the careless and evasive swearing of daily speech.

Matthew's crowd praises God for giving authority ‘to men’, plural. Many interpreters read the phrase as Matthew's pointer to the church, to which the risen Jesus entrusts the ministry of forgiveness (16:19, 18:18, John 20:23). Traditions differ on how that authority is exercised, through ordained ministers in confession and absolution, through the preaching of the gospel, or through the whole community's discipline, but all find its source in the Son of Man's own authority.

The verse imagines a community with prophets and righteous teachers among it and gives every member a share in their work through hospitality. Those who support the church's servants take part in the ministry they support.

The circle of disciples around Jesus is the first picture of the church as a family. Doing the Father's will (compare 7:21) is the mark of membership, and the risen Jesus will call his disciples ‘My brothers’ (28:10).

Whether the field is taken as the world (verse 38) or, with Augustine and Calvin, also as the visible church, the command forbids the servants to do the final sorting themselves. It has been read as a charter against persecuting dissenters (Roger Williams) and against demanding a church of the pure (Augustine against the Donatists). It does not cancel the limited discipline Jesus gives the church in 18:15-17, but it puts final separation beyond the servants' reach.

Jesus says outright that the field is the world, which is why the Donatists and later Roger Williams read the parable as being about society at large. Augustine replied that the kingdom of verse 41, from which the angels gather offenses, must be the church as it now exists, since no offenses can be gathered from the kingdom in its final glory (City of God 20.9). The verse can carry both readings: the good seed are sons of the kingdom scattered through the world, and the visible community of Jesus' followers is not exempt from the mixture.

Calvin (Institutes 4.1.13) used the net, with the weeds, to argue that the visible church contains the good and the bad until the end, against those who sought a church of the perfect. The image fits the church's mission as fishing (4:19), which gathers widely and does not sort its catch before the time.

The verse contributes three things to the doctrine of the church on which Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Christians agree: the church belongs to Christ (‘My church’), Christ himself builds it (‘I will build’), and death will not destroy it. They differ over what the rock is and whether Peter's role continues in an office, as the chapter note sets out; those are second-order questions on which faithful Christians disagree and remain brothers.

What is bound and loosed on earth corresponds to what is bound and loosed in heaven. The church's decisions carry heaven's weight only when they agree with Christ's word; Jesus' rebuke of Peter in verse 23 shows that the one who received the keys could still speak from ‘the things of men’.

The community is not measured by the ninety-nine who stay but by its care for the one who wanders. The parable makes pursuing straying believers a charge to the whole church and not only to its leaders, and it stands immediately before the instructions on correction in verses 15 to 17, which are meant to serve the same end.

The church's first response to sin between members is a private, honest conversation aimed at restoration. The verse rules out both ignoring the sin and spreading it abroad, and it measures success by whether the brother is won, not by whether the offended party is vindicated.

The gathered church has a real responsibility for its members' lives, and its judgment carries weight. Yet the verse's last words must be read in Matthew, whose Jesus ate with tax collectors and called one to follow him (9:9-11). To treat someone as a tax collector is to recognize that he has put himself outside and must be sought again, not to license contempt or cruelty; Paul says the same when he tells the church not to regard such a person as an enemy but to warn him as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:15).

The authority first promised to Peter is here exercised by the community, which suggests to many interpreters that Peter received it as the representative of the disciples; Catholic interpreters hold that the two passages describe the authority of the whole college of apostles together with a particular role for Peter within it. All agree that the church's decisions in discipline and forgiveness are meant to carry heaven's weight when they are faithful to Christ, as John 20:23 says of forgiving and retaining sins.

The gathered company is mixed until the king examines it, as the field has wheat and weeds and the net good and bad fish until the end of the age (13:30, 13:47-50). The church is not a society of the already good; it is filled from the roads, and the sorting belongs to the king.

The disciples' community is a family of brothers and sisters under one Teacher. Jesus has already defined his family as those who do his Father's will (12:50), and after the resurrection he calls the disciples ‘my brothers’ (28:10). Teaching remains a gift in the church (Ephesians 4:11), but no teacher stands above the rest as a rival to Christ.

The women who followed and served are the continuity between Jesus' ministry, his death, and his resurrection: they see him die, see where he is laid, and find the tomb empty. The church's first witnesses to the core of the gospel, that he died, was buried, and was raised, were these women (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

The first community of the risen Lord is formed by his word of restoration: the disciples who failed are named his brothers and summoned to meet him. The church is from its beginning a family of forgiven deserters gathered by Christ's invitation (Hebrews 2:11).

The eleven gather at Jesus' appointment, not their own. The church's assembly around the risen Lord begins as obedience to his word, and it is to this reduced and doubting group that the whole mission of the church is given.
The Twelve are called first to presence and then to mission. The order matters: those who are sent must first have been with him, and the authority they carry is his, not their own.

The new family of Jesus is formed around him and defined by doing God's will. The verse gives the church its first name for itself as a household of brothers and sisters, a name the New Testament letters use constantly.

Jesus refuses to make belonging to the disciples' circle the test of belonging to him. The church has drawn on this saying to recognize the work of Christ beyond its own boundaries. Matthew 12:30, where whoever is not with Jesus is against him, is the other side of the same truth: toward Jesus himself there is no neutrality, but toward those who act in his name the disciples must be generous.

The hundredfold houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children are received in this age, which points to the new family of Jesus' followers (3:34-35). Many commentators note that fathers do not appear among what is received: in this family God alone is Father (11:25), and no one takes the place of patriarch.
The household with its servants and doorkeeper has often been read as a picture of the church in the time between Christ's going and his return, with every member given a task.

The first witnesses of the burial, and then of the empty tomb, are women whose testimony counted for little in their world. God builds the church's witness to the resurrection on people others would have discounted.
Jesus forms a new leadership for a renewed Israel. The Twelve are both the foundation of the church and a sign that Jesus is regathering the people of God.

Jesus refuses to make belonging to the disciples' circle the test of genuine work done in his name. Luke balances this with the opposite saying in 11:23, ‘Whoever is not with Me is against Me’, spoken about neutrality toward Jesus himself. Together they distinguish loyalty to Jesus, which is required, from loyalty to one group of his followers, which is not.

The disciples are a little flock, few and exposed, yet the heirs of God's kingdom. The image of the flock connects them with Israel under God the shepherd (Isaiah 40:11, Ezekiel 34) and anticipates the church of Acts.

The father's last word is ‘your brother’. The open ending asks whether the faithful son will accept his returned brother at the same table, the very issue Luke's churches faced with tax collectors, sinners, and Gentiles (Acts 11:1-18), and which every congregation faces when the prodigal comes home.

The bride belongs to Christ. The Old Testament pictured God as Israel's husband (Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2:19-20), and the New Testament calls the church Christ's bride (Ephesians 5:25-27, Revelation 21:2). John places himself outside the marriage as its servant, a stance that belongs to every ministry.

Confessing Jesus as the Christ can cost a person a community. John writes so that later believers who faced exclusion would see themselves in this man and know that Jesus seeks out the one who has been cast out (9:35), a warning and comfort Jesus repeats in 16:2.

The flock is formed by recognition of a voice. Belonging to Christ's people is not first a matter of enclosure or membership but of hearing and following him, which is why the man cast out of the synagogue in chapter 9 is found among the sheep.

The church's unity comes from one shepherd, not from one enclosure. Most interpreters read the other sheep as Gentiles who will believe, gathered with Jewish disciples into one flock, the gathering John names in 11:52 and Paul describes in Ephesians 2:14-16.

The phrase ‘into one’ anticipates Jesus' prayer that his followers may be one (17:21) and his saying about one flock and one shepherd (10:16). The unity of Jews and Gentiles in one people is a result of the cross, not of human agreement.
The visible sign of the community is not its doctrine, power, or numbers but its mutual love. The world is meant to recognize Jesus in how his people treat one another (17:21-23).

The community of Jesus is defined by the command given to it. Mutual love is not one duty among many for the church but the purpose of its whole life together, and the next verse sets that love against the world's hatred.

The unity Jesus asks for is modeled on the unity of the Father and the Son and kept by the Father's name. It is not a unity the disciples create by agreement but one they are kept in by God, which is why it is a petition before it is a command.

The church of every age is included in Jesus' prayer on the night before his death. Its faith comes through the apostles' word, which is why the church has always understood itself as apostolic, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20).

Christians agree that this unity is God's gift and will, and differ on its form. The Catholic Church teaches that the unity Christ prayed for subsists in the Catholic Church and seeks full visible communion with other Christians; the Orthodox Church holds that unity is given in the one apostolic faith and Eucharist of the church that has kept them. Many Protestants distinguish a spiritual unity already given in Christ from the visible structures of the churches and seek unity in the gospel, while ecumenical Protestants have worked toward visible union or toward reconciled diversity among churches that remain distinct. All read the verse as a petition that judges the church's divisions.

From the cross Jesus binds together his mother and his disciple as mother and son. The scene is filial care, and it is also the first household of the new family formed by his death, those born of God (1:12-13) who receive one another. Catholic teaching also finds here Mary given as mother to the church (Lumen Gentium 58); Protestant readers generally stress Jesus' care and the new community of disciples.

The risen Christ entrusts his church with declaring forgiveness. Traditions differ on how this is exercised: Catholic and Orthodox teaching connects it with priestly absolution in the sacrament of penance (Council of Trent, session 14), Lutheran teaching with the office of the keys in preaching and absolution (Augsburg Confession 28), and many Protestants with the proclamation of the gospel to which all believers bear witness. All agree that the authority is Christ's and the forgiveness is God's.

Whatever the number means, John stresses that the net held all the fish without tearing. The fathers read the unbroken net, like the untorn tunic, as a picture of the church's unity; the text itself shows the Lord's gathering as abundant and whole.
The church is formed by people who receive the word and are baptized into the community. From its first day, belonging to Christ and belonging to his people go together.

The church's life is built on apostolic teaching, shared life, the breaking of bread, and prayer. The list describes what the Spirit-filled community did, and it has served churches of every tradition as a picture of their own gatherings.
The church grows because the Lord adds to it. Luke credits the growth to Christ, not to the apostles' strategy, and describes the saved as those being added to the community.
The church is defined first by God's love and call, and holiness is given before it is achieved. Paul will spend chapters 6 and 12-15 on how saints live, but here he establishes that they are saints.
Faith is built up in company. Paul does not picture himself as a supplier and the Romans as consumers; believers strengthen one another's faith by sharing it.

The vessels of mercy are a people called from Jews and Gentiles together. Verse 24 turns the argument from the patriarchs to the present church, which is the evidence that God's word has not failed (verse 6).

Given the factions of chapters 1 to 4, where Corinthians rallied behind Paul, Apollos, or Cephas, Paul's insistence that all the apostles preach the same thing is pointed. The church's unity rests on one received gospel, not on loyalty to a favorite teacher.

Separation at the table spread through the community. A leader's fear shaped others' conduct, and the result was two classes of believers in one church. Paul treats the fracture of fellowship as a gospel issue, not a question of manners.

‘The truth of the gospel’ (verses 5 and 14) is not only a doctrine to be believed but a way to walk. For Paul a church that divides at the table by ethnicity denies the gospel it confesses, whatever its creed.

The church is one body in which ethnicity, legal status, and sex do not rank members before God. Egalitarian readers take this as a principle extending to all roles in church and home; complementarian readers take it as equal standing in salvation, with other texts governing roles. Both agree it forbids second-class membership.

If ‘his inheritance in the saints’ means God's inheritance, then the church is what God counts as his treasure, as Israel was his portion (Deuteronomy 32:9). The people of God are valuable to God, not only blessed by him.
Christ's rule over all things is ‘for the church’. His lordship over the cosmos serves his people, and the church lives under a head who governs everything that could threaten it.
The church is Christ's body, the place where his fullness dwells. It is not an optional association of individual believers but the community in which the risen Christ is present in the world.
The church is not a merger of two existing groups but a new creation, one humanity made in Christ. Its unity across the deepest division of the ancient world is itself a creation of God.
The church is both a commonwealth and a household. The Gentiles are not guests but full citizens and family, with the same standing before God as the people of Israel who believe.

The church's foundation is apostolic and prophetic testimony, with Christ as the stone that fixes everything. Traditions differ on whether the foundation is laid once (the apostolic witness preserved in Scripture) or continues in an apostolic office, but all agree Christ is the stone on which it rests.

The church is called to honor people whose service costs them, not because of rank but because they display the mind of Christ. Paul's instruction heads off any suspicion that Epaphroditus returned early in failure.
The one who rules creation is the head of the church. The church's life depends on its connection to him (2:19), and his headship over it anticipates his rule over everything.
Believers are ‘holy brothers’ and partners in a calling that comes from heaven. The church is defined by that shared calling and by a common confession, not by ethnicity or place.
The church is God's house, the household over which the Son presides. Membership is described in terms of continuing confidence and hope, not only of past entry.
The community is responsible for each member's faith. Daily encouragement is presented as one of the means God uses to keep people from hardening.

Perseverance is not a private achievement. The gathered church is the setting in which believers stir one another up and encourage one another, and abandoning it is treated as a step toward the drift the letter warns against.

The twelve stars tie the woman to the twelve tribes, and the heavenly clothing shows how God sees his people even while, on earth, they are in labor, hunted, and hidden. Her glory is given, not earned: she is clothed with it.

The woman, now clearly the persecuted community after the Messiah's ascension, is carried as Israel was carried out of Egypt. The church lives through a limited season of pursuit, and God sets both its length and its protection.

The woman's other children are defined by two marks: obedience to God's commandments and loyalty to Jesus' testimony. The church in Revelation is the offspring of Genesis 3:15, in the line of the one who crushes the serpent and therefore the target of his hatred.
